Deployment

The project site, the hosted server, and the Worker.

Project Site (GitHub Pages)

The static site in website/ is published to https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/ by .github/workflows/pages.yml.

  • A push to main runs the website tests, builds _site from website/, and deploys the artifact with actions/deploy-pages.
  • workflow_dispatch republishes the site from the Actions tab without a code change.
  • Pages is configured with the "GitHub Actions" source, so there is no gh-pages branch. Removing pages.yml stops all publishing and the site returns 404.
  • The github-pages environment only allows deployments from main.

Hosted MCP Server

The server is deployed via Horizon Prefect, Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents.

Test Chat (UI)

Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser:

https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat

MCP Server Endpoint

Integrate via the MCP protocol at:

https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp

[!IMPORTANT] Authentication is required to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a client.

Hosted Studio

The Living Studio SPA is deployed to Cloudflare Workers:

Environment URL
Production (main) https://agentic-odi.alehar.workers.dev/
Pull request preview Posted automatically by Cloudflare Workers Builds as a PR comment

Production deploys on every push to main. The Worker is agentic-odi; keep name in wrangler.jsonc aligned with the Worker connected in the dashboard. Preview builds run for non-production branches and are ephemeral: the Cloudflare PR comment is the source of truth, so do not copy a preview URL into docs. The hosted UI loads without a backend; canvas data, chat, and mutations need the sidecar tunnel described below.

Living Studio on a Free Cloudflare Worker

Workers Containers — the only way to run the Python sidecar entirely on Cloudflare — requires the Workers Paid plan. On the free plan, the Worker serves the built SPA as Workers Static Assets and proxies /api/* to the sidecar through a free, account-less Cloudflare Quick Tunnel.

wrangler.jsonc publishes apps/studio/dist with SPA fallback and runs the Worker first for /api/*; infra/cloudflare/worker.ts forwards those calls to the SIDECAR_URL secret. The browser only talks to the Worker origin, so the sidecar's CORS list is not involved.

+

Every response from the Worker — static assets and proxied API calls alike — +carries a content security policy (default-src 'self', connect-src 'self', +frame-ancestors 'none') plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, +X-Frame-Options: DENY, a strict referrer policy, and a Permissions Policy that +disables geolocation, camera, and microphone. tests/test_worker_security_headers.py +pins those headers so a preview deployment can be smoke-tested against them.

# 1. Build the SPA that the Worker uploads as static assets
 npm --prefix apps/studio ci
 npm --prefix apps/studio run build
 
 # 2. Terminal A — MCP server (:8000) + sidecar (:8100)
 python scripts/dev.py
 
 # 3. Terminal B — free public URL for the sidecar (no account required)
 cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8100
 # copy the https://<random>.trycloudflare.com URL it prints
 
 # 4. Store the URL on the Worker, then deploy
 npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL   # paste the trycloudflare URL
 npx wrangler deploy

Workers Builds settings (Workers & Pages → your Worker → Settings → Builds):

Setting Value
Production branch main
Root directory /
Build command npm --prefix apps/studio ci && npm --prefix apps/studio run build
Deploy command npx wrangler deploy
Preview command npx wrangler preview

A Worker has no run command: the Worker script runs on Cloudflare. Set name in wrangler.jsonc to the Worker you created before the first deploy.

Pull request previews

Workers Builds posts the build status and Preview URL to the pull request automatically. To enable it:

  1. Open the Worker → Settings → Build → Branch control.
  2. Keep the production branch set to main and enable Preview Builds.
  3. If Cloudflare shows Set up Worker Previews, complete the one-time switch. This cannot be reversed.
  4. Confirm the Preview command is npx wrangler preview.

wrangler.jsonc must keep a previews block, even an empty one: the wrangler preview command fails the build with "Your Wrangler configuration is missing a previews block" without it. Assets and compatibility settings stay at the top level, so "previews": {} is enough while Previews need no extra settings. If a future Preview needs vars or bindings, add them under previews with Preview-safe values.

Previews do not inherit production settings. The SPA loads from a Preview, but /api/* returns 502 SIDECAR_URL is not configured until a preview-specific SIDECAR_URL secret is configured:

npx wrangler preview secret put SIDECAR_URL --name <branch>

When --name is omitted it defaults to the current git branch. Previews are ephemeral, and pull requests from forks may not receive one. If Cloudflare does not comment, paste the URL into the PR's Deployment section.

The cf CLI can inspect build triggers and recent builds (cf builds triggers list, cf builds list) and create a Preview (cf previews deploy), but it does not post GitHub PR comments. The Workers Builds Git integration owns the PR link; cf is only an optional verification tool and requires cf auth login.

[!NOTE] The sidecar runs on your machine, so the Worker only works while python scripts/dev.py and the Quick Tunnel are running. Quick Tunnel URLs change on every restart — update the secret with npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL. Chat also needs a reachable OpenAI-compatible endpoint in the Studio's Settings; the canvas, job map, and impact simulation work without one.

Lint, types, frontend checks, and the coverage map.

Everything below mirrors what CI runs. Install the workspace first:

uv sync --all-packages

Linting, Formatting & Type Checks

Shared tooling lives in the root pyproject.toml, so one command covers every Python project:

uv run ruff check .
 uv run ruff format --check .
-uv run mypy apps packages
+uv run mypy apps brand packages
 uv run --directory website mypy .
 
 # Security scanning
 uv run bandit -c pyproject.toml -r apps packages website/

Frontend & Desktop Checks (studio)

The SPA and Tauri shell mirror their CI jobs locally:

npm --prefix apps/studio run lint       # ESLint
 npm --prefix apps/studio run typecheck  # tsc --noEmit
 npm --prefix apps/studio test -- --run  # Vitest (run once)
 npm --prefix apps/studio run build      # production build → apps/studio/dist
 cd apps/studio/src-tauri && cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo check

Conversational UI coverage

The agent-composed surfaces and the first-run tour are covered at these levels:

File What it covers
apps/studio/src/ui/protocol.test.ts Spec parsing: prop types, enums, ranges, required props, depth/node/size ceilings, unknown types
apps/studio/src/ui/UiRenderer.test.tsx Card rendering, computed opportunity scores, action dispatch, per-node failure isolation, catalog/registry parity
apps/studio/src/components/chat/Conversation.test.tsx Prose and surfaces interleaved in the agent's order; card actions become messages
apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_ui_spec.py Catalog validation and render_ui tool-schema generation
apps/studio-api/tests/test_studio_chat_ui.py render_ui interception, ui SSE events, and the correction fed back to the model

apps/studio/src/onboarding/machine.test.ts Tour transitions, no forward motion without a goal, versioned storage, malformed records
apps/studio/src/onboarding/FirstRunWizard.test.tsx Auto-open, full flow to a destination, skip/Escape, focus trap, resume, replay, inline model repair, flag off

Website Checks (GitHub Pages)

The website/ static site is part of the main CI workflow. Its tests assert the committed OG art is reproducible, that index.html stays in sync with the README, and that the publish pipeline (website/tests/test_pages_deploy.py) still exists:

uv run --directory website pytest tests/

Publishing happens in .github/workflows/pages.yml: it runs those tests, builds _site from website/, and deploys the artifact with actions/deploy-pages on every push to main. There is no gh-pages branch, so that workflow is the only thing that keeps https://alehar9320.github.io/agentic-odi/ online.

Formatting workflow

  • When editing Python files, either rely on the pre-commit hooks below (recommended) or run Ruff formatting directly before pushing:

    uv run ruff format .

  • CI behavior:

    • CI runs uv run ruff check . to lint without modifying files.
    • CI runs uv run ruff format --check . to verify formatting only.
    • If CI fails on formatting, run uv run ruff format . locally, commit the changes, and push again.

Pre-commit hooks

To run the checks automatically before each commit:

uv tool install pre-commit
 pre-commit install

After this, ruff and ruff-format run on staged files whenever you commit. You can also trigger them manually:

pre-commit run --all-files

Testing

Tests use pytest with pytest-asyncio (strict mode) and run entirely in-memory — no running server required. Tests live next to the package they cover, and every test runs from the repository root:

uv run pytest                        # everything
 uv run pytest apps/cli               # one app
 uv run pytest packages/core          # one package
 uv run pytest tests/contract         # cross-package contracts
 uv run pytest tests/scripts          # dev launcher

The MCP server contract test compares the live FastMCP registry with packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py, so add or change a tool in both places. The CLI local-backend contract test keeps _LOCAL_HANDLERS aligned with the same tool names.

Test Coverage

CI runs the suite on Python 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12 and uploads one combined coverage.xml from the 3.12 job to Codecov.

The Codecov upload authenticates with the CODECOV_TOKEN repository secret and is non-blocking (fail_ci_if_error: false), so a Codecov outage or a fork PR without secrets cannot fail the test job. The badge at the top of the README tracks main, which is the baseline every PR is compared against:

  • Project status requires at least 90% coverage (target: 90%) and tolerates a 1% dip from codecov.yml.
  • Patch status is informational for now, so new code can land while the suite catches up.

To reproduce the report locally:

uv run pytest \
   --cov=agentic_odi_cli \
   --cov=agentic_odi_connectors \
   --cov=agentic_odi_core \
   --cov=agentic_odi_mcp_server \
   --cov=agentic_odi_studio_api \
   --cov-report=term-missing \
   --cov-report=xml:coverage.xml

[!NOTE] Coverage is only collected for the Python packages. apps/studio/ and test directories are excluded in codecov.yml.

Conventions

  • Test files live under each project's tests/ directory and are named test_*.py.
  • Root tests/ is reserved for cross-package checks (contract/ and scripts/).
  • Every async test is decorated with @pytest.mark.asyncio.
  • Use Client(mcp) directly (no HTTP server needed) for fast, isolated tests.
  • The MCP server's reset_db autouse fixture clears in-memory state before each test.

apps/studio-api/tests/ Health, config, canvas, SSE chat, SPA fallback, MCP hydration, probes, and step/outcome passthrough

[!TIP] Type /test in the AI assistant to have the agent run all tests and report the results automatically.

Agent Session Tracking

Agent sessions are captured with the Entire CLI. The repository integration lives in .entire/settings.json, .cursor/hooks.json, and .opencode/plugins/entire.ts. Run entire status to confirm it is enabled and entire checkpoint list to inspect captured checkpoints.

The chat-first interface, its first run, and the desktop app.

The Living Studio is the conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation: an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous agent connected to the MCP server.

The Studio runs three ways locally, plus a hosted deployment. All of them serve the same SPA, which talks only to the sidecar on http://127.0.0.1:8100 — the SPA never contacts MCP or the LLM directly.

Interface

The Studio opens as a conversation, not a dashboard.

Surface What it does
First-run tour A four-step, skippable welcome on the very first visit: what the studio is, which ambition brought you here, the live state of your sidecar/MCP/model (with inline repair when the model is down), and the first move. The four doors are I have one in mind, My boss handed me a priority, Help me find the next one, and Pressure-test a bet; each starts the matching conversation. Replay it from Settings → Replay the welcome tour.
First run A short conversation in the chat, not a form: what you are building, who feels the problem, the job they are trying to get done, then where it hurts. One question at a time, with a reflection before the next ask, quick replies, and Explore on my own always visible. Skipping is allowed; answers and progress are kept as a draft. Re-open it any time with /start, the home stage's context pill, or Settings.
Hero One rotating headline above the composer: a greeting (time of day, plus your name if you set one in Settings), the product/job you set up, what is already on the canvas, or an intent-first prompt such as What are you trying to win this quarter? It cycles every few seconds and stays still under prefers-reduced-motion.
Suggestion pills Below the headline. Sharpen an opportunity always starts a conversation; the next pill becomes Pressure-test a bet once outcomes exist, or Find the next opportunity before that. Capture what you heard replaces the landscape pill once a job exists. They change as the canvas fills up.
Composer Docked at the bottom of the transcript. Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line, Cmd/Ctrl+K focuses it, and / opens the command palette. The send button becomes a stop button while a reply streams.
Bar The only persistent chrome: home, new conversation, catch-up, live model status, and settings. There is no navigation drawer to compete with the thread.
Rail Above the conversation, and only once the thread has produced something: Landscape · N, Job map · N, Evidence · N, What I know · N. Every item is derived from the canvas and the memory, so the strip is a record of the work rather than a fixed menu.
Lens A view docks to the right of the thread on wide screens and becomes a full-height sheet on narrow ones. The transcript and the composer stay on screen and stay usable; Esc, Close, or the rail chip closes it. Every lens ends in one sentence that re-enters the conversation — Ask which to chase, Walk me through the job, Weigh the evidence — so leaving a view is never a return to a menu. Settings and catch-up use the same lens.

Replies render Markdown (headings, lists, emphasis, inline and fenced code). Tool calls appear inline as small trace chips while the agent works.

Slash commands

Type / to open the palette. Up/Down move, Enter or Tab runs the selected command, Esc closes it. Commands are handled in the SPA and never call the model, so they work when it is offline.

Command Effect
/help Every command, as a notice in the transcript
/start Resume the context conversation
/new New conversation
/home Return to the empty stage
/jobs Job summary, then the job map
/landscape, /jobmap, /evidence, /settings Open that lens beside the conversation
/impact, /capture Start the conversation that produces the card. /capture falls back to the offline form when no model answers.
/status Model, MCP, context, and canvas status

Unknown commands produce a transcript notice pointing at /help.

The welcome tour

The tour is the front door, the context conversation is the first room. It is skippable at every step (Skip the tour or Escape), resumable (progress is stored after every transition in localStorage["studio.onboarding"]), and replayable from Settings.

Everything lives in apps/studio/src/onboarding/:

File Role
content.ts Steps and goal copy as typed data — the only place the words live
machine.ts Pure state transitions, no React or storage
storage.ts Versioned, defensive localStorage persistence
OnboardingProvider.tsx Auto-open, persistence, replay
FirstRunWizard.tsx, steps.tsx, onboarding.css The dialog
../features/flags.ts The firstRunWizard toggle

App.tsx only wires the provider and the wizard around the existing shell; the chat, canvas, and sidecar code are untouched.

Toggling the tour

firstRunWizard defaults to on. Resolution order, highest first:

Source Example Use
Query parameter ?flags=firstRunWizard:off QA a build without rebuilding
Local override localStorage["studio.flags.firstRunWizard"] = "off" Per-browser opt-out
Build environment VITE_STUDIO_FIRST_RUN_WIZARD=off npm --prefix apps/studio run build Ship it dark
Default on

Accepted values are 1/0, true/false, on/off, yes/no, and enabled/disabled. With the flag off, no dialog renders, no onboarding state is written, and Settings hides the replay action.

Guidance, not gates

The setup conversation is a nudge, never a prerequisite. If you skip it, the home stage keeps a dashed Tell me what you're building pill; it reopens the conversation exactly where you left off. /start and Settings do the same. The conversation also understands a natural reply: say "skip", "not now", or "show me the landscape" and it reacts instead of recording it as an answer. When a brief exists, it opens on a review and asks what changed rather than asking everything again.

Without a model

When the LLM is unreachable the Studio keeps working:

  • A Working by hand strip explains the state and offers capture, job map, and context.
  • Messages still return deterministic ODI guidance from the sidecar, labelled Local guidance.
  • Jobs can be created, renamed, and deleted; steps added, edited, and removed; outcomes recorded, re-scored, and removed. All of it goes through the same local repository the model uses.
  • Settings → Base URL and Model reconnect the assistant whenever you are ready.

The user's context is sent with every chat request, so the assistant starts from the product, audience, job, and problem rather than asking for them again.

The thread is the room

Capture, scoring, simulation, and decisions are conversations. The storefront never asks the PM to leave the thread to do work: the agent asks for the customer's words or the bet in plain language, then renders the surface that carries it. A lens exists for reading and for people who prefer a click, not for doing the work.

That is also enforced in the agent's system prompt: it is told to keep every artifact in the conversation, never to send the PM to a panel, and to end each reply with the next move as an action on the surface.

What it remembers

The studio keeps a small, local, editable model of the person it is helping. It is not a profile and not a transcript index; it is the handful of things that change the next answer.

Kind What it captures
career The PM's role, remit, and what success looks like for them
opportunity The opportunity or bet currently in play
business Goals, metrics, and commercial constraints
stakeholder Who else matters and what they care about
constraint Time, budget, policy, or technical limits
evidence What has actually been heard or measured
preference How the PM likes to work and be spoken to

Each note is suggested or confirmed. Suggested notes appear first under What I know with Yes, that's right, That's not it, and Edit; confirmed notes can be edited or forgotten. The PM can also add a note by hand. Nothing is silently promoted: the agent may propose, but the person decides.

The agent writes notes through a remember tool during a normal reply. The sidecar applies it, emits a memory SSE event, and the panel updates without a refresh. Memory writes are best-effort — a database failure never turns a good answer into an error.

Storage is a separate SQLite file from the ODI repository: ~/.agentic-odi/studio.db, overridable with AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DB (:memory: is supported and is what the tests use). The API is small:

Method Path Purpose
GET /api/memory/observations Everything the agent believes
POST /api/memory/observations Add a note by hand
PATCH /api/memory/observations/{id} Edit text, confidence, or status
DELETE /api/memory/observations/{id} Forget one note
DELETE /api/memory Forget all notes and conversations

Forget everything is a two-step confirmation and also clears the visible thread, because the server deletes the conversations behind it.

The thread comes back

Conversations are stored beside the memory. On launch the SPA asks GET /api/conversations/latest, restores that thread's user and assistant turns, and continues with the same conversation_id on the next message. New conversation starts a fresh one without touching the memory; Forget everything removes both. The composer stays usable while the restore is in flight, and a restore failure simply leaves the room empty.

Rich responses

The copilot does not only talk. When a surface carries the evidence better than a paragraph, the agent renders one inline in the conversation: a scored outcome, a ranked opportunity board, a before/after simulation of a bet, a customer quote with its lineage, the eight-stage job map, an opportunity thesis, or a decision record. Three properties keep this safe and cheap to extend:

  • The catalog is closed and owned by the SPA. apps/studio/src/ui/catalog.ts declares nine primitives and seven cards, their JSON Schema props, and the description the model reads. There is no HTML, no eval, and no third-party component in the path. Prose is rendered by the same Markdown component the transcript already used.
  • The sidecar is catalog-agnostic. The SPA sends the catalog with each turn; the sidecar derives the render_ui tool schema from it, validates what comes back, and streams a ui SSE event. Invalid props return to the model as a tool result naming the exact violation, and the loop offers the tool again, so a fumbled prop is corrected in the same reply. A client that sends no catalog never sees the tool.
  • Cards are views, never actors. Every button is an intent string that the agent receives as the user's next message — one authority, one audit trail.

A surface is one node tree, streamed as one event:

{
   "type": "outcome-card",
   "props": {
     "id": "O-1",
     "statement": "Minimize the time it takes to propagate secrets across environments",
     "importance": 9,
     "satisfaction": 3
   }
 }

The opportunity thesis is the intent-first card: one opportunity with its importance, satisfaction, the gap in plain words, the thesis itself, and the smallest next move. It is the shape the agent reaches for when the PM is deciding what to chase, rather than when they are inspecting a single score.

The conversation keeps the order the agent produced: a delta appends to the open prose part, a ui event opens a card, and the next delta opens a new paragraph after it. The opportunity score is computed from importance and satisfaction when the agent omits it, so the ODI formula has exactly one home (src/lib/odi.ts). Unknown component types degrade to a quiet fallback; a tree that fails validation is dropped whole, and the surrounding prose still reads.

Adding a surface

  1. Add an entry to CATALOG in apps/studio/src/ui/catalog.ts — props as a JSON Schema subset, plus the description the model will read.
  2. Register the component in apps/studio/src/ui/registry.ts.
  3. Implement it in apps/studio/src/ui/cards.tsx (domain shape) or apps/studio/src/ui/primitives.tsx (composition).
  4. Run npm --prefix apps/studio test. The registry parity test fails if the catalog and the registry drift apart.

No server change is needed, and no new dependency.

Desktop signing & updater secrets

Self-updating and code signing are env-driven: if a secret is absent, an unsigned artifact is produced instead of failing. CI reads these from GitHub Actions secrets.

Secret Purpose
TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY Signs updater artifacts (.sig) and the latest.json manifest. A tagged release fails loudly without it. Generate with npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri signer generate.
TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD Password for the private key (optional when the key has none).
APPLE_CERTIFICATE / APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD macOS Developer ID certificate (base64 .p12) and its password.
APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY macOS signing identity.
APPLE_ID / APPLE_PASSWORD / APPLE_TEAM_ID macOS notarization credentials.
WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE / WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD Windows Authenticode PFX (base64) and its password; imported by CI and injected into the bundle config.

Releases are published by .github/workflows/tauri-release.yml when a v* tag is pushed. The desktop app checks for updates on startup and via Settings → Check for updates.

Managing the updater signing key

The updater key pair authenticates release artifacts so an installed app can verify that an auto-update genuinely came from you. The public key is embedded in apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json (plugins.updater.pubkey) and is safe to commit. The private key must never be committed, logged, printed in CI, or attached to a build artifact.

  1. Generate a key pair (only if you need a new one). Leave -p "" for a passwordless key, or pass a password and remember it:

    npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri signer generate -- -w ./living-studio.key -p "" -f

    This writes living-studio.key (private, 0600) and living-studio.key.pub (public).

  2. Paste the public key into apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json:

    {
   "plugins": {
     "updater": {
       "endpoints": ["https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/latest.json"],
       "pubkey": "<contents of living-studio.key.pub>"
     }
   }
 }

  3. Store the private key outside the repository (the repo root is git-tracked; a sibling directory is not), with restricted permissions:

    mkdir -p ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys && chmod 700 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys
 mv living-studio.key ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/
 chmod 600 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key

    Move it to a long-term secret store (password manager, 1Password/Bitwarden/ Vault, or a private encrypted backup) when you decide where that lives. Losing it means future releases can no longer be signed for existing installs.

  4. Add the private key as a GitHub Actions secret (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret), or via the CLI:

    gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY < ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
 gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD --body ""   # only if you set a password

  5. Verify the secrets exist (values are never displayed):

    gh secret list

  6. Rotate by repeating steps 1–4, then publishing a release signed with the new key. Existing installs still verify against the public key compiled into their binary, so keep the old private key usable and publish the new public key ahead of the cut-over.

[!CAUTION] If the private key leaks, treat auto-updates as compromised: generate a new pair, rotate the Actions secret, and publish a freshly signed release.

The problem

Opinion is expensive.

Roadmaps set by whoever talks loudest.

Decisions default to seniority, not evidence.

Features for customers who never asked.

Nobody validated the outcome; only the idea.

Agents fluent in everything, grounded in nothing.

A model will confidently invent your customer.

Add it up and the roadmap isn't a plan. It's a guess.

The method

Ask for outcomes, not opinions.

Outcome-Driven Innovation asks customers how much each desired outcome matters and how satisfied they are with it today.

The gap between importance and satisfaction is where products win or die.

Agentic ODI stores those outcomes, scores them, and serves them to any agent over MCP.

Opportunity = importance + max(importance - satisfaction, 0)

86% innovation success rate — as reported in ODI literature (Strategyn)

How it works

Three moves, one loop.

Talk

One room. Describe a job, or paste what a customer said. The studio captures jobs, steps, and desired outcomes from plain language — and every score stays editable by hand.

Ask

Any agent calls the same MCP tools the studio uses: job maps, outcomes, evidence, opportunity scores. Thirty tools, at decision time, from your own machine or the hosted server.

Steer

The team decides from the same picture. Scored outcomes, opportunity boards, and bet simulations, composed inline by the agent and reviewable by a human.

Connectors

Bring your own tools.

The studio reads from where your customer evidence already lives. 16 presets ship today, and the registry takes your own MCP or REST server in the same shape.

</EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

Then announce "Using [skill] to [purpose]" and follow the skill exactly. If it has a checklist, create a todo per item.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent it. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## Platform Adaptation

If your harness appears here, read its reference file for special instructions:

- Kiro: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/kiro-tools.md`
- Freebuff: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/freebuff-tools.md`
- Claude Code: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/claude-code-tools.md`
- Codex: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/codex-tools.md`
- Pi: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/pi-tools.md`
- Antigravity: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/antigravity-tools.md`
- Hermes Agent: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/hermes-tools.md`
- Muse: `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/muse-tools.md`

## User Instructions

User instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, etc, direct requests) take precedence over skills, which in turn override default behavior. Only skip skill workflows or instructions when your human partner has explicitly told you to.

## Kiro Tool Mapping

Skills speak in actions, not tool names. On Kiro CLI they resolve as follows:

| Action skills request | Kiro CLI equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| Invoke or load a skill | Read the skill's `SKILL.md` with the `read` tool and follow its instructions directly |
| Create a todo / mark one complete | `todo_list` (create, add, complete, remove commands) |
| Read a file | `read` tool (Line or Directory mode) |
| Create or overwrite a file | `write` tool (create command) |
| Edit a file in place | `write` tool (strReplace command) |
| Delete, move, or rename a file | `shell` tool (`rm`, `mv`) |
| Run a shell command | `shell` tool |
| Search file contents | `grep` tool (regex pattern search) |
| Search by symbol / semantic code search | `code` tool (search_symbols, pattern_search, etc.) |
| Find files by name | `glob` tool |
| List a directory | `read` tool (Directory mode) |
| Fetch a URL | `web_fetch` tool |
| Search the web | `web_search` tool |
| Ask your human partner a question | Respond to the user in your message |
| Dispatch a subagent (`Subagent (general-purpose):` template) | `subagent` tool with a `kiro_default` stage (blocking mode) |
| Enter plan mode | `todo_list` to track steps; write designs to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` |
| Persist progress across compaction | Write the ledger and briefs under `.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/` (see `executing-plans`) |

Skills live in `.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md`. Kiro has no automatic skill-loading tool — read a `SKILL.md` with the `read` tool before following it.

For the full Kiro tool reference including subagent dispatch patterns and git worktree instructions, read `.agents/skills/using-superpowers/references/kiro-tools.md`.
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>

- Superpowers artifacts belong under `docs/superpowers/`: designs in `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, plans in `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>.md`.
- Run `uv run pytest` from the root; see `.agents/workflows/test.md` and `docs/architecture/testing.md` for focused commands.

display.text:
name: Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

# Publishing needs `pages: write` and an OIDC token so the deploy can be
# attributed to this workflow run.
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Pages allows one deployment at a time. Never cancel a run mid-deploy.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      # Gate the deploy on the site contract so a broken page never goes live.
      - name: Pytest (website)
        run: uv run --directory website pytest tests/

      # The site is generated from the repository's own sources, so it is
      # built here rather than copied. website/dist/ is the committed copy a
      # reviewer reads; this step produces the artifact that goes live.
      - name: Build site
        run: uv run python website/tools/build_site.py --out _site

      - name: Configure Pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v6

      - name: Upload Pages artifact
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: _site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

input.newString:
- uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      # Fail fast if any critical source file is missing before we build.
      # A deleted website/index.html or build_site.py must never let a
      # broken site reach GitHub Pages.
      - name: Verify critical source files exist
        run: |
          for f in \
            .github/workflows/pages.yml \
            website/tools/build_site.py \
            website/index.html \
            website/tests/test_pages_deploy.py; do
            [ -s "$f" ] || { echo "::error::Missing or empty critical file: $f"; exit 1; }
          done
          echo "OK: critical source files present"

      # Gate the deploy on the site contract so a broken page never goes live.
      - name: Pytest (website)
        run: uv run --directory website pytest tests/

      # The site is generated from the repository's own sources, so it is
      # built here rather than copied. website/dist/ is the committed copy a
      # reviewer reads; this step produces the artifact that goes live.
      - name: Build site
        run: uv run python website/tools/build_site.py --out _site

      # Refuse to upload an empty or broken artifact. A missing index.html or
      # 404.html means the build produced nothing usable; stop before deploy.
      - name: Verify the built site is non-empty
        run: |
          for f in _site/index.html _site/404.html; do
            [ -s "$f" ] || { echo "::error::Built site missing or empty: $f"; exit 1; }
          done
          echo "OK: built site contains index.html and 404.html"

      - name: Configure Pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v6

      - name: Upload Pages artifact
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: _site

name: Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

# Publishing needs `pages: write` and an OIDC token so the deploy can be
# attributed to this workflow run.
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Pages allows one deployment at a time. Never cancel a run mid-deploy.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup

      # Gate the deploy on the site contract so a broken page never goes live.
      - name: Pytest (website)
        run: uv run --directory website pytest tests/

      # Fail fast if any critical source file is missing before we build.
      # A deleted website/index.html or build script must never let a
      # broken site reach GitHub Pages.
      - name: Verify critical source files exist
        run: |
          for f in \
            .github/workflows/pages.yml \
            website/tools/build_site.py \
            website/index.html \
            website/tests/test_pages_deploy.py; do
            [ -s "$f" ] || { echo "::error::Missing or empty critical file: $f"; exit 1; }
          done
          echo "OK: critical source files present"

      # The site is generated from the repository's own sources, so it is
      # built here rather than copied. website/dist/ is the committed copy a
      # reviewer reads; this step produces the artifact that goes live.
      - name: Build site
        run: uv run python website/tools/build_site.py --out _site

      # Refuse to upload an empty or broken artifact. A missing index.html or
      # 404.html means the build produced nothing usable; stop before deploy.
      - name: Verify the built site is non-empty
        run: |
          for f in _site/index.html _site/404.html; do
            [ -s "$f" ] || { echo "::error::Built site missing or empty: $f"; exit 1; }
          done
          echo "OK: built site contains index.html and 404.html"

      - name: Configure Pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v6

      - name: Upload Pages artifact
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: _site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

**What was added** (in `.worktrees/ci-pages-pre-deploy-safety-gate`, branch `ci/pages-pre-deploy-safety-gate`):

Two safety-gate steps in `.github/workflows/pages.yml`:

1. **Verify critical source files exist** — runs after `pytest`, before `build_site.py`. Fails fast if `pages.yml`, `build_site.py`, `website/index.html`, or `test_pages_deploy.py` is missing or empty.

2. **Verify the built site is non-empty** — runs after `build_site.py --out _site`, before `upload-pages-artifact`. Fails if `_site/index.html` or `_site/404.html` is missing or empty, refusing to upload a broken artifact.

This is defense in depth alongside PR #187 (which fails CI red when a protected file is deleted). Now even if a bad commit slips past CI, the Pages workflow won't publish an empty or broken site.
